lessons.title: The Cloud Collapses
lessons.goal: Measure particle degeneracy with the effective sample size and watch it fall.
lessons.theory:
Run the reweighting a few times without doing anything else and the set bleeds out. The particles far from the reading get weights near zero and stop contributing, so most of the memory you paid for is carrying nothing, and every further reading concentrates what is left.

There is a number for it. The **effective sample size** is `1.0 / (weights ** 2).sum()`, and it says how many particles are really contributing. It starts at the full count when all weights are equal and falls towards one as the weight concentrates.

Print it after each of five updates on the same reading. Four thousand particles drawn uniformly over ten metres fall to about 150 effective ones on the first reading, because a sensor with sigma 0.05 has already ruled out almost the whole corridor, and then keep sliding towards 70. That is not a tuning problem, it is what repeated multiplication does.

The standard rule is to act when the effective size falls below half the count. The action is resampling, which is the next lesson, and this number is what triggers it. A particle filter without this check works in the demo and dies in the corridor.

lessons.title: Resampling
lessons.goal: Redraw the particle set in proportion to its weights and restore the effective sample size.
lessons.theory:
Resampling replaces the weighted set by an unweighted one that represents the same belief. Draw `N` particles from the current set, each one chosen with probability equal to its weight, and reset every weight to `1.0 / N`. Heavy particles get copied several times, light ones disappear.

Implemented with a cumulative sum it is three lines: `cumulative = np.cumsum(weights)`, draw uniform numbers, and `np.searchsorted` to find which particle each number lands on.

The effective sample size jumps back to the full count. That number is now honest again in the sense that all particles carry equal weight, and dishonest in another: many of them are copies of each other. Resampling does not create information, it redistributes attention, and the count of **unique** values in the set is the thing to watch. Print it and you will see a few thousand samples collapse to a few hundred distinct positions.

That loss is why you resample only when the effective size demands it, and why the prediction step, which jitters every particle with its own noise, is what restores diversity afterwards.

import numpy as np

STANDOFF = 1.00
RANGE_SIGMA = 0.05
COUNT = 4000
Z = 2.2361


def effective(weights):
    return 1.0 / float((weights ** 2).sum())


def reweight(particles, weights, z):
    expected = np.sqrt(particles ** 2 + STANDOFF ** 2)
    out = weights * np.exp(-0.5 * ((z - expected) / RANGE_SIGMA) ** 2)
    return out / out.sum()


def resample(particles, weights, rng):
    cumulative = np.cumsum(weights)
    picks = rng.uniform(0.0, 1.0, particles.size)
    index = np.searchsorted(cumulative, picks)
    chosen = particles[np.clip(index, 0, particles.size - 1)]
    return chosen, np.full(particles.size, 1.0 / particles.size)

particles = rng.uniform(-5.0, 5.0, COUNT)
weights = np.full(COUNT, 1.0 / COUNT)
for _ in range(3):
    weights = reweight(particles, weights, Z)
print("before  effective", round(effective(weights), 2), "unique positions", np.unique(particles).size)
particles, weights = resample(particles, weights, rng)
print("after   effective", round(effective(weights), 2), "unique positions", np.unique(particles).size)
print("mean after resampling", round(float(particles.mean()), 4))

lessons.title: Reading an Answer Out of a Cloud
lessons.goal: Compare the weighted mean, the most likely particle and the mean of the dominant cluster.
lessons.theory:
The set is the belief, but the rest of the stack wants a number. There are three honest ways to produce one and they disagree, which is information rather than a nuisance.

The **weighted mean** is the best estimate in the least squares sense, and it is the one that lands in the empty valley when the belief has two peaks.

The **most likely particle** is the highest weighted sample. It is always somewhere the robot could be, and it jitters, because it is one sample rather than an average.

The **dominant cluster mean** splits the set, keeps the heaviest group, and averages inside it. It costs more, and it is what you want when a navigator has to commit to one side of an obstacle.

The demonstration builds a two peak belief where 70 percent of the weight sits near plus two, prints all three answers, and then prints how much weight lives within ten centimetres of each. Read the last line before choosing which estimator to publish.

lessons.title: The Particle Filter, Boxed
lessons.goal: Package the particle filter and resolve an ambiguity that defeats the extended filter.
lessons.theory:
`ParticleFilter` holds the particles and their weights. `predict(distance, sigma)` moves every particle and jitters it. `update(z)` reweights and resamples when the effective size falls below half. `estimate()` returns the weighted mean and its spread.

The mission is the ambiguous corridor. The robot starts two metres past the anchor and drives away from it, and the only sensor is the lateral range. The first reading admits two answers, so nothing can be decided from it. Then the robot moves, and the readings that follow only fit one of the two: from the far side the range grows, from the near side it would have shrunk first.

The particle filter starts with both explanations, kills the wrong one after a couple of metres of driving, and converges. An extended filter initialised on the wrong peak stays there for the whole run, because a Gaussian cannot hold a second hypothesis long enough for the evidence to arrive.

Read the two final errors. That gap is the reason this chapter exists, and it is also the honest cost sheet: eight thousand particles to beat two numbers, worth paying only when the belief is genuinely not a bell curve.
lessons.task: Complete `predict` and `update` in `ParticleFilter`, then read its error against the extended filter that guessed the wrong side.
lessons.starter:
import math
import numpy as np

STANDOFF = 1.00
RANGE_SIGMA = 0.05
STEP = 0.05
STEPS = 120
START = 2.00
COUNT = 8000


class ParticleFilter:
    def __init__(self, particles, rng):
        self.particles = particles
        self.weights = np.full(particles.size, 1.0 / particles.size)
        self.rng = rng

    def predict(self, distance, sigma):
        # TODO: move every particle and give each its own noise
        return self.particles

    def update(self, z):
        expected = np.sqrt(self.particles ** 2 + STANDOFF ** 2)
        # TODO: reweight by the likelihood, then normalise
        self.weights = self.weights
        if 1.0 / float((self.weights ** 2).sum()) < self.particles.size / 2.0:
            cumulative = np.cumsum(self.weights)
            index = np.searchsorted(cumulative, self.rng.uniform(0.0, 1.0, self.particles.size))
            self.particles = self.particles[np.clip(index, 0, self.particles.size - 1)]
            self.weights = np.full(self.particles.size, 1.0 / self.particles.size)
        return self.weights

    def estimate(self):
        mean = float((self.particles * self.weights).sum())
        return mean, math.sqrt(float((self.weights * (self.particles - mean) ** 2).sum()))


rng = np.random.default_rng(885)
pf = ParticleFilter(rng.uniform(-5.0, 5.0, COUNT), rng)
ekf_x, ekf_P = -2.00, 0.25
truth = START
for k in range(STEPS):
    truth = truth + STEP
    z = math.sqrt(truth * truth + STANDOFF * STANDOFF) + float(rng.normal(0.0, RANGE_SIGMA))
    pf.predict(STEP, 0.01)
    pf.update(z)
    ekf_x = ekf_x + STEP
    ekf_P = ekf_P + 0.0001
    expected = math.sqrt(ekf_x * ekf_x + STANDOFF * STANDOFF)
    H = ekf_x / expected
    S = H * ekf_P * H + RANGE_SIGMA ** 2
    K = ekf_P * H / S
    ekf_x = ekf_x + K * (z - expected)
    ekf_P = (1.0 - K * H) * ekf_P
mean, spread = pf.estimate()
print("true position", round(truth, 3))
print("particle filter", round(mean, 3), "spread", round(spread, 3), "error", round(abs(mean - truth), 3))
print("extended filter", round(ekf_x, 3), "sigma", round(math.sqrt(ekf_P), 3), "error", round(abs(ekf_x - truth), 3))

import math
import numpy as np

STANDOFF = 1.00
RANGE_SIGMA = 0.05
STEP = 0.05
STEPS = 120
START = 2.00
COUNT = 8000


class ParticleFilter:
    def __init__(self, particles, rng):
        self.particles = particles
        self.weights = np.full(particles.size, 1.0 / particles.size)
        self.rng = rng

    def predict(self, distance, sigma):
        self.particles = self.particles + distance + self.rng.normal(0.0, sigma, self.particles.size)
        return self.particles

    def update(self, z):
        expected = np.sqrt(self.particles ** 2 + STANDOFF ** 2)
        w = self.weights * np.exp(-0.5 * ((z - expected) / RANGE_SIGMA) ** 2)
        self.weights = w / w.sum()
        if 1.0 / float((self.weights ** 2).sum()) < self.particles.size / 2.0:
            cumulative = np.cumsum(self.weights)
            index = np.searchsorted(cumulative, self.rng.uniform(0.0, 1.0, self.particles.size))
            self.particles = self.particles[np.clip(index, 0, self.particles.size - 1)]
            self.weights = np.full(self.particles.size, 1.0 / self.particles.size)
        return self.weights

    def estimate(self):
        mean = float((self.particles * self.weights).sum())
        return mean, math.sqrt(float((self.weights * (self.particles - mean) ** 2).sum()))


rng = np.random.default_rng(885)
pf = ParticleFilter(rng.uniform(-5.0, 5.0, COUNT), rng)
ekf_x, ekf_P = -2.00, 0.25
truth = START
for k in range(STEPS):
    truth = truth + STEP
    z = math.sqrt(truth * truth + STANDOFF * STANDOFF) + float(rng.normal(0.0, RANGE_SIGMA))
    pf.predict(STEP, 0.01)
    pf.update(z)
    ekf_x = ekf_x + STEP
    ekf_P = ekf_P + 0.0001
    expected = math.sqrt(ekf_x * ekf_x + STANDOFF * STANDOFF)
    H = ekf_x / expected
    S = H * ekf_P * H + RANGE_SIGMA ** 2
    K = ekf_P * H / S
    ekf_x = ekf_x + K * (z - expected)
    ekf_P = (1.0 - K * H) * ekf_P
mean, spread = pf.estimate()
print("true position", round(truth, 3))
print("particle filter", round(mean, 3), "spread", round(spread, 3), "error", round(abs(mean - truth), 3))
print("extended filter", round(ekf_x, 3), "sigma", round(math.sqrt(ekf_P), 3), "error", round(abs(ekf_x - truth), 3))
lessons.hint: `predict` adds the distance and a noise draw of the same size as the set, and `update` builds `w` from the likelihood before normalising it.

lessons.title: The State the Whole Stack Reads
lessons.goal: Define the published estimate record and fill it from the state and its covariance.
lessons.theory:
The project is the estimator of a warehouse delivery robot. Differential drive, wheel odometry, a cheap MEMS gyro, and three UWB anchors bolted to the racking at known positions. One state, one covariance, one record published to everything else on the robot.

The state is four numbers: `[px, py, theta, gyro_bias]`. Position because the planner needs it, heading because the controller needs it, and the gyro bias because leaving it out is what chapter six showed you cannot afford.

The published record is not the state. It is what the rest of the stack is allowed to depend on: the pose, a single position sigma that a planner can inflate its margins with, the heading sigma, and a health flag. Publishing the raw covariance matrix invites five subsystems to interpret it five ways.

`sigma_xy` here is the radius of the uncertainty, `math.sqrt(P[0, 0] + P[1, 1])`, which is the number to compare against a corridor width. Publish that and the planner never has to know what a covariance is.

lessons.title: The Prediction Core
lessons.goal: Predict the four state robot from wheel speed and a gyro that carries a bias.
lessons.theory:
The prediction runs at 50 Hz off the odometry and the gyro. Wheel speed goes in as `v`, the gyro gives a turn rate, and the filter subtracts its own bias estimate before using it:

`theta = theta + (gyro - bias) * dt`

The transition Jacobian is the four by four identity with three entries written. Two of them you already know from chapter five, the heading feeding into `px` and `py`. The third is new and it is the one that makes the bias observable at all: `F[2, 3] = -dt`, which says that an error in the bias estimate turns into a heading error at one radian per radian per second per second.

Without that entry the covariance never links heading to bias, the gain on the bias row stays zero, and the state sits at whatever you initialised it to while pretending to be estimated.

The run here predicts for five seconds with no anchors at all, sixty times over, and prints the root mean square drift next to the sigma the filter claims. The drift has to fit inside that sigma, and this model comes out comfortably inside because the odometry noise is white and largely averages out over 250 steps. If the drift ever exceeds the claimed sigma, the filter is lying before a single measurement has arrived, and there is no point continuing until it does not.
lessons.task: Complete `move` and `transition` for the four state model, then compare the drift after five blind seconds against the sigma.
lessons.starter:
import math
import numpy as np

DT = 0.02
BLIND_STEPS = 250
V_TRUE = 0.60
GYRO_BIAS = 0.030
V_SIGMA = 0.020
GYRO_SIGMA = 0.010
Q = np.diag([0.0000002, 0.0000002, 0.00000005, 0.0000000001])


def omega_at(t):
    return 0.40 * math.sin(2.0 * math.pi * t / 20.0)


def move(x, v, omega, dt):
    theta = float(x[2, 0])
    # TODO: roll the pose forward and leave the bias alone
    return x.copy()


def transition(x, v, dt):
    theta = float(x[2, 0])
    F = np.eye(4)
    F[0, 2] = -v * math.sin(theta) * dt
    F[1, 2] = v * math.cos(theta) * dt
    # TODO: the entry that lets a bias error become a heading error
    return F


def blind_run(seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    truth = np.array([[1.0], [1.0], [0.0], [GYRO_BIAS]])
    x = np.array([[1.0], [1.0], [0.0], [0.0300]])
    P = np.diag([0.010 ** 2, 0.010 ** 2, 0.010 ** 2, 0.004 ** 2])
    for k in range(1, BLIND_STEPS + 1):
        omega = omega_at(k * DT)
        truth = move(truth, V_TRUE, omega, DT)
        v_meas = V_TRUE + float(rng.normal(0.0, V_SIGMA))
        gyro = omega + GYRO_BIAS + float(rng.normal(0.0, GYRO_SIGMA))
        F = transition(x, v_meas, DT)
        x = move(x, v_meas, gyro - float(x[3, 0]), DT)
        P = F @ P @ F.T + Q
    drift = math.hypot(float(x[0, 0]) - float(truth[0, 0]), float(x[1, 0]) - float(truth[1, 0]))
    return drift, math.sqrt(float(P[0, 0]) + float(P[1, 1])), abs(float(x[2, 0]) - float(truth[2, 0]))


drifts = [blind_run(4242 + s) for s in range(60)]
rms_drift = math.sqrt(sum(d[0] ** 2 for d in drifts) / len(drifts))
print("blind for", BLIND_STEPS * DT, "seconds, over", len(drifts), "runs")
print("worst drift", round(max(d[0] for d in drifts), 4))
print("rms drift", round(rms_drift, 4), "claimed sigma_xy", round(drifts[0][1], 4))
print("worst heading error", round(max(d[2] for d in drifts), 5))

lessons.title: The Anchors Speak
lessons.goal: Update the four state filter from three UWB ranges and watch the uncertainty collapse.
lessons.theory:
Three anchors sit on the racking at known coordinates and answer at 10 Hz. Each one gives a range, which is nonlinear in the state, so each one gets the extended update from chapter five with a row that has two live columns:

`H = np.array([[dx / r, dy / r, 0.0, 0.0]])`

The zeros matter. A range says nothing about heading directly, and nothing about the gyro bias, so those columns are zero and the gain on them comes entirely from the correlations the prediction step builds. That is the same mechanism that let a position measurement correct velocity in chapter four, working two states further away.

Three anchors are the minimum worth having. Two leave a mirror ambiguity around the line joining them, which is precisely the two peak belief of chapter eight, and an extended filter handles that badly. Three, not in a line, resolve it.

Apply them one at a time rather than stacking, for the reason from chapter four: they arrive when they arrive, and a sequential update is the same answer.

import math
import numpy as np

RANGE_SIGMA = 0.05
R = np.array([[RANGE_SIGMA ** 2]])
ANCHORS = [(0.0, 0.0), (10.0, 0.0), (5.0, 8.0)]
TRUE = (3.400, 1.250)


def range_update(x, P, z, anchor):
    dx = float(x[0, 0]) - anchor[0]
    dy = float(x[1, 0]) - anchor[1]
    r = math.sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy)
    H = np.array([[dx / r, dy / r, 0.0, 0.0]])
    y = np.array([[z - r]])
    S = H @ P @ H.T + R
    K = P @ H.T @ np.linalg.inv(S)
    x = x + K @ y
    A = np.eye(4) - K @ H
    P = A @ P @ A.T + K @ R @ K.T
    return x, P


rng = np.random.default_rng(4243)
x = np.array([[3.100], [1.500], [0.310], [0.0290]])
P = np.diag([0.300 ** 2, 0.300 ** 2, 0.020 ** 2, 0.004 ** 2])
print("start   sigma_xy", round(math.sqrt(float(P[0, 0]) + float(P[1, 1])), 4),
      "position error", round(math.hypot(float(x[0, 0]) - TRUE[0], float(x[1, 0]) - TRUE[1]), 4))
for anchor in ANCHORS:
    z = math.hypot(TRUE[0] - anchor[0], TRUE[1] - anchor[1]) + float(rng.normal(0.0, RANGE_SIGMA))
    x, P = range_update(x, P, z, anchor)
    print("anchor at", anchor, "sigma_xy", round(math.sqrt(float(P[0, 0]) + float(P[1, 1])), 4),
          "position error", round(math.hypot(float(x[0, 0]) - TRUE[0], float(x[1, 0]) - TRUE[1]), 4))
lessons.hint: The row is the unit vector to the anchor padded with two zeros, and the rest is the extended update with the Joseph form.

value: P = A @ P @ A.T + K @ R @ K.T

lessons.title: The Gate on the Door
lessons.goal: Reject multipath ranges with a chi squared gate and measure what it saves.
lessons.theory:
UWB in a warehouse is a bouncing sport. Racking is steel, a range that took the long way round arrives a metre or two too long, and it happens on a few percent of readings. Those are not noise, they are wrong answers, and no `R` describes them.

The gate from chapter seven goes on the door of the range update. Compute the NIS, compare against 3.841, and drop anything above it. A rejected reading costs nothing except a slightly larger covariance until the next one arrives, and there are thirty ranges a second.

The run injects a 1.5 m multipath error into 3 percent of readings and scores the estimator with and without the gate. Read the RMSE and the rejection count together: the gate throws away roughly one reading in twenty even when nothing is wrong, and that is the price of the 95 percent threshold, not a fault.

Publish the rejection rate. A robot whose rejection rate climbs from 8 percent to 50 percent as it enters a particular aisle has just told you something about that aisle that no other instrument will.
lessons.task: Complete the gate inside the range update, then compare the two RMSE numbers and the two rejection counts.
lessons.starter:
import math
import numpy as np

DT = 0.02
STEPS = 1500
V_TRUE = 0.60
GYRO_BIAS = 0.030
RANGE_SIGMA = 0.05
MULTIPATH = 1.5
CHI2_95 = 3.841
R = np.array([[RANGE_SIGMA ** 2]])
ANCHORS = [(0.0, 0.0), (10.0, 0.0), (5.0, 8.0)]
Q = np.diag([0.0000002, 0.0000002, 0.00000005, 0.0000000001])


def omega_at(t):
    return 0.40 * math.sin(2.0 * math.pi * t / 20.0)


def move(x, v, omega, dt):
    theta = float(x[2, 0])
    return np.array([[float(x[0, 0]) + v * math.cos(theta) * dt],
                     [float(x[1, 0]) + v * math.sin(theta) * dt],
                     [theta + omega * dt],
                     [float(x[3, 0])]])


def transition(x, v, dt):
    theta = float(x[2, 0])
    F = np.eye(4)
    F[0, 2] = -v * math.sin(theta) * dt
    F[1, 2] = v * math.cos(theta) * dt
    F[2, 3] = -dt
    return F


def run(gated):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(4242)
    truth = np.array([[1.0], [1.0], [0.0], [GYRO_BIAS]])
    x = np.array([[1.0], [1.0], [0.0], [0.0]])
    P = np.diag([0.10 ** 2, 0.10 ** 2, 0.05 ** 2, 0.05 ** 2])
    total, counted, rejected = 0.0, 0, 0
    for k in range(1, STEPS + 1):
        omega = omega_at(k * DT)
        truth = move(truth, V_TRUE, omega, DT)
        v_meas = V_TRUE + float(rng.normal(0.0, 0.020))
        gyro = omega + GYRO_BIAS + float(rng.normal(0.0, 0.010))
        F = transition(x, v_meas, DT)
        x = move(x, v_meas, gyro - float(x[3, 0]), DT)
        P = F @ P @ F.T + Q
        if k % 5 == 0:
            for anchor in ANCHORS:
                true_r = math.hypot(float(truth[0, 0]) - anchor[0], float(truth[1, 0]) - anchor[1])
                z = true_r + float(rng.normal(0.0, RANGE_SIGMA))
                if rng.uniform() < 0.03:
                    z = z + MULTIPATH
                dx = float(x[0, 0]) - anchor[0]
                dy = float(x[1, 0]) - anchor[1]
                r = math.hypot(dx, dy)
                H = np.array([[dx / r, dy / r, 0.0, 0.0]])
                y = np.array([[z - r]])
                S = H @ P @ H.T + R
                score = float((y.T @ np.linalg.inv(S) @ y)[0, 0])
                # TODO: when gated, count the rejection and skip this reading
                K = P @ H.T @ np.linalg.inv(S)
                x = x + K @ y
                A = np.eye(4) - K @ H
                P = A @ P @ A.T + K @ R @ K.T
        if k > 250:
            total = total + (float(x[0, 0]) - float(truth[0, 0])) ** 2 + (float(x[1, 0]) - float(truth[1, 0])) ** 2
            counted = counted + 1
    return math.sqrt(total / counted), rejected


for gated in (False, True):
    rmse, rejected = run(gated)
    print("gated", gated, "position rmse", round(rmse, 4), "readings rejected", rejected)

lessons.title: The Bias the Gyro Hides
lessons.goal: Show what the estimator does with and without the gyro bias in the state.
lessons.theory:
The MEMS gyro on this robot is worth about two dollars and it reads 0.030 rad/s when the robot is standing still. That is 1.7 degrees per second, which after a minute of driving is a heading error of a hundred degrees if nothing corrects it.

Two versions of the same estimator, differing by one state. The first has `gyro_bias` in the state, subtracts it before integrating, and lets the anchors teach it what the bias is. The second assumes the gyro is honest.

The numbers are not close. With the bias state the position RMSE is about a centimetre and the estimated bias converges to within a fraction of a milliradian per second of the truth. Without it the heading is wrong by more than a radian and the position error is measured in metres, because the anchors keep correcting the position while the model keeps steering the prediction into the wrong direction.

That is the lesson of the whole course in one comparison. The filter is not what makes the estimate good. The **model** is, and a filter can only estimate what you gave it a state for.
lessons.task: Complete the bias handling in the prediction, then compare the two runs on bias, heading and RMSE.

lessons.title: The Whole Refinery
lessons.goal: Run the full estimator for a minute and sign it off against every test in the course.
lessons.theory:
Everything at once. Sixty seconds of driving, prediction at 50 Hz off odometry and the gyro, three anchors at 10 Hz with multipath, a gate on the door, four states including the bias.

The sign off is four numbers and each one comes from a different chapter:

- **position RMSE** from chapter zero, the score that says whether the estimate is any good
- **coverage** from chapter zero, the fraction of the run where the truth sat inside two sigma, and it has to be near 0.95 or higher
- **mean NIS** from chapter seven, near 1.0, the one test that will still work tomorrow on the real robot where there is no truth
- **rejection rate** from chapter seven, a few percent, so the gate is filtering and not strangling

A filter that passes all four is not merely accurate. It is accurate and it knows how accurate it is, which is the difference between an estimate you can plan on and a number that happens to be right.

Run it, read the four lines, and the mission verdict at the end.

lessons.title: When Estimation Is the Wrong Tool
lessons.goal: Compare tuning the filter against changing the hardware and recommend the cheaper fix.
lessons.theory:
A filter extracts what the measurements contain. It cannot manufacture information that was never there, and once it is near that limit the only way forward is more information.

So when somebody asks for a better estimate, there are four moves and only two of them are yours:

- **tune the filter**, which is free and usually worth a small factor
- **add a state**, which is free and worth an enormous factor when something real was unmodelled, like the gyro bias in the last lesson
- **a better sensor**, which costs money and buys error roughly in proportion, until some other source becomes the floor
- **more readings per second**, which costs bandwidth and buys about the square root

The run measures the last three on the same mission. Read the table. Moving `Q` by a factor of ten in either direction makes the estimate worse, because the baseline was already tuned, so there is nothing left there. Anchors five times better buy a factor of two and a half, not five, because the odometry noise has become part of the floor. Doubling the anchor rate buys about fifteen percent. That is the signature of a filter at its information limit, and at that point another week of tuning is a week thrown away.

The last row is the one to remember. Nothing here beats bolting the gyro to the chassis properly, which costs an afternoon and removes the vibration that all four of these were fighting.
